sets.title: Set 1: Original Exam Questions
sets.description: The original MCQs from the June 2025 Class Health Care Support Assistant College Final Exam, Cicely McDonnell College of Health Sciences (19 November 2025), Multiple Choice Questions Q1 to Q20.

questions.text: The cholera stool is described as:
questions.explanation: Rice water (B) is correct because cholera, caused by Vibrio cholerae, produces sudden, profuse, painless watery diarrhoea that is pale grey and cloudy with flecks of mucus, resembling water in which rice has been washed, often with a fishy smell. The patient can lose up to a litre of fluid an hour, so severe dehydration and shock develop quickly. The priority is rapid rehydration with oral rehydration salts (ORS) or IV fluids, strict hand hygiene and safe disposal of stool. Bloody stool (A) is typical of dysentery (shigellosis, amoebic dysentery). Sticky stool (C) is not a recognised description of cholera. Mucoid stool (D) is seen in dysentery and some inflammatory bowel conditions, but in cholera mucus is only present as small flecks.

questions.text: In a given town with a population of 30,000, an outbreak of influenza occurred in 2024. During the month of January, 200 cases were reported, in March 50 more cases were reported and in July another 50 cases were reported. No new cases were reported in the rest of the year. What was the prevalence of influenza in this town in 2024?
questions.explanation: 1% (B) is correct. Prevalence is the total number of cases in a population divided by the population at risk, multiplied by 100. The total number of cases reported in 2024 is 200 + 50 + 50 = 300. Prevalence = 300 / 30,000 x 100 = 1%. The other options come from wrong arithmetic: 0.8% (A) would mean only 240 cases, 8.3% (C) would mean about 2,500 cases, and 10% (D) would mean 3,000 cases. (The original paper wrote "cholera" in the last line of this question although the outbreak described is influenza; it has been corrected here so the question reads consistently.)

questions.text: Typhoid can be prevented by:
questions.explanation: Safe handling of food (A) is correct because typhoid fever, caused by Salmonella Typhi, spreads by the faecal-oral route through food and water contaminated by the faeces or urine of a patient or carrier. Prevention therefore rests on food hygiene (washing hands before preparing food, cooking food thoroughly, keeping food covered), drinking safe boiled or treated water, proper sanitation and typhoid vaccination in high-risk groups. Use of sterile equipment (B) prevents blood-borne infections such as HIV and hepatitis B, not typhoid. Ciprofloxacin (C) is a treatment, not a routine preventive drug, and routine prophylaxis would promote antibiotic resistance. Oral rehydration salt (D) treats the dehydration caused by diarrhoea but does not prevent the infection.

questions.text: A vector borne disease includes:
questions.explanation: Malaria (C) is correct because it is transmitted by a vector, the female Anopheles mosquito, which carries the Plasmodium parasite from one person to another when it bites. A vector is a living organism (usually an insect) that transmits an infectious agent. Control measures include sleeping under insecticide-treated nets, indoor residual spraying, draining stagnant water and early treatment. Cholera (A) and typhoid (B) are food- and water-borne diseases spread by the faecal-oral route. Brucellosis (D) is a zoonosis acquired from infected animals through raw milk or direct contact with animal products, not through a vector.

questions.text: Amoebic dysentery can be prevented by:
questions.explanation: Environmental hygiene (B) is the best answer because amoebic dysentery, caused by Entamoeba histolytica, spreads by the faecal-oral route when cysts from human faeces contaminate food, water and hands. Control therefore depends mainly on environmental sanitation: safe disposal of human faeces (latrines), protection of water sources from contamination, control of flies and, together with it, personal and food hygiene. Food hygiene (A) is also a useful measure and is the closest alternative; if your lecture notes list it as the key answer for this question, follow your notes. Drinking chlorinated water (C) is not reliable because amoebic cysts resist the levels of chlorine used for ordinary water treatment; boiling or filtering is more effective. Immunization (D) is incorrect because there is no vaccine against amoebiasis.

questions.text: Mucolytic drugs are best prescribed in treatment of:
questions.explanation: Chronic bronchitis (C) is correct because mucolytics (such as acetylcysteine, carbocisteine, bromhexine and ambroxol) thin and loosen thick, sticky bronchial secretions so they can be coughed up more easily. They are therefore used where thick sputum is a problem, for example chronic bronchitis, COPD and bronchiectasis. Patients should drink plenty of fluids to help loosen secretions. Asthma (A) is mainly treated with bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids, and mucolytics may irritate the airways and trigger bronchospasm. Atelectasis (B) is lung collapse, managed by deep breathing, incentive spirometry and positioning. Pharyngitis (D) is throat inflammation and is not caused by thick bronchial mucus.

questions.text: The correct definition of high blood pressure is:
questions.explanation: BP of 140/90 mmHg or higher (D) is correct because hypertension is diagnosed when readings taken on repeated occasions are 140/90 mmHg or above; this is the threshold used by the WHO and the Kenyan Ministry of Health guidelines, which is the standard HCA and nursing students in Kenya are examined on. A reading of 110/70 (A) is normal, 120/80 (B) is the normal upper limit, and 130/80 (C) is the cut-off used in the American (ACC/AHA) guidelines, not the one used in this setting. The HCA should measure the blood pressure correctly, record it accurately and report abnormal readings to the nurse.

questions.text: The role of the HCA in managing patients with non-communicable disease is to:
questions.explanation: Educate patients (C) is correct because the health care assistant works under the supervision of the nurse and supports patients with non-communicable diseases (hypertension, diabetes, asthma and others) through health education: encouraging adherence to medication, a healthy diet with less salt and sugar, regular exercise, stopping smoking and alcohol, and keeping clinic appointments. The HCA also observes and reports changes to the nurse. Prescribing medications (A) and making diagnoses (B) are outside the HCA's scope of practice and belong to the clinician. Referral (D) is a clinical decision made by the nurse or clinician; the HCA reports concerns rather than refers.

questions.text: A complication of diabetes is:
questions.explanation: Heart failure (B) is correct because long-standing high blood sugar damages blood vessels and the heart muscle, leading to macrovascular complications such as coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, stroke and heart failure. Other complications include retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy and diabetic foot ulcers. Obesity (A) is mainly a risk factor for type 2 diabetes rather than a result of it. Hypertension (C) commonly coexists with diabetes and is a major risk factor for its complications, but it is usually described as a coexisting condition rather than a complication. Asthma (D) is not related to diabetes.

questions.text: A characteristic symptom of asthma is:
questions.explanation: Respiratory wheeze (B) is correct because in asthma the airways become inflamed, swollen and narrowed by bronchospasm and mucus, so air moving through them produces a high-pitched whistling sound, mainly on breathing out. Other typical features are cough (often worse at night), shortness of breath and chest tightness, usually triggered by allergens, cold air, exercise or infection. Sudden loss of vision (A) points to eye or neurological emergencies, severe headache and vomiting (C) to raised intracranial pressure or migraine, and frequent nosebleeds (D) to clotting problems, hypertension or nasal conditions.

questions.text: Which type of hypertension occurs with no known cause?
questions.explanation: Primary hypertension (C), also called essential hypertension, is correct because it has no identifiable single cause and accounts for about 90 to 95% of cases; it is linked to age, family history, obesity, high salt intake, physical inactivity, stress, smoking and alcohol. Secondary hypertension (A) results from an identifiable cause such as kidney disease, endocrine disorders (for example Cushing's syndrome, phaeochromocytoma) or certain drugs. Tertiary (B) and quaternary (D) hypertension are not recognised types.

questions.text: Which of the following terms in a transmission cycle is used to describe a habitat in which the agent normally lives, grows, and multiplies?
questions.explanation: Reservoir (C) is correct because the reservoir is the natural habitat of the infectious agent where it lives, grows and multiplies; it may be a human (patient or carrier), an animal, or the environment (water, soil). It is one link in the chain of infection: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry and susceptible host. The portal of exit (A) is the route by which the agent leaves the reservoir (for example faeces, respiratory secretions, blood). The portal of entry (B) is the route by which it enters a new host (for example mouth, broken skin, respiratory tract). The susceptible host (D) is the person who can become infected because of low resistance.

questions.text: Which of the following is the correct sequence for donning of the personal protective equipment?
questions.explanation: Gown, mask, goggles, gloves (B) is correct because the standard donning order starts with the gown to cover clothing, then the mask or respirator, then eye protection (goggles or face shield), and finally gloves, which go on last so that they cover the cuffs of the gown and stay clean until entering the patient area. Doffing (removal) is done in the order of most contaminated first: gloves, goggles or face shield, gown, then mask, followed by hand hygiene. Options A, C and D place gloves or goggles before the gown or mask, which would contaminate the items put on later or leave the gown cuffs uncovered.

questions.text: An HCA student is assisting in feeding of patient YY. The patient states that he is full and is unable to finish the food. The appropriate bin for disposing the remaining food is:
questions.explanation: Black bin (A) is correct because leftover food is general, non-hazardous (non-infectious) waste, and in the colour-coded waste segregation system used in Kenyan health facilities the black bin is for this kind of waste, together with paper, packaging and other non-contaminated items. The red bin (B) is used for infectious waste such as contaminated dressings and items soiled with blood or body fluids (the colour for infectious waste, red or yellow, varies between facilities). The purple bin (C) is for cytotoxic or other special hazardous waste. The white bin (D) is not used for food waste. Correct segregation at the point of generation reduces infection risk and disposal costs.

questions.text: Examples of disinfectants include:
questions.explanation: Sodium hypochlorite, Bactoguard (A) is correct because disinfectants are chemicals used on inanimate objects and surfaces (floors, beds, equipment, spills) to destroy micro-organisms. Sodium hypochlorite (bleach, jik) is a chlorine disinfectant, and Bactoguard cleaner is a quaternary-ammonium surface disinfectant. Antiseptics, by contrast, are used on living tissue such as skin. Option B mixes a surface disinfectant (Bacteranios) with an antiseptic (Hibitane, chlorhexidine in spirit). Option C mixes a chlorine disinfectant (Presept) with an antiseptic (Betadine, povidone-iodine). Option D contains skin and hand antiseptics (Hibiscrub, chlorhexidine-based). Only option A has two items that are both disinfectants.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about alcohol hand-rub?

options.A: It should be performed before a surgical procedure
options.C: Should be performed when hands are visibly soiled
options.D: Hands should be rinsed after performing it

questions.explanation: It should take 20-30 seconds (B) is correct because the WHO technique for routine alcohol-based hand rub requires enough product to cover all hand surfaces and rubbing the hands for 20 to 30 seconds until they are dry. Surgical hand preparation (A) is a separate procedure, done as a surgical scrub or surgical hand rub that takes longer, so this is not the best statement about routine hand rub. When hands are visibly soiled (C) they must be washed with soap and water (taking 40 to 60 seconds), because alcohol does not work well in the presence of dirt or organic matter. Hands are not rinsed (D) after an alcohol rub; the product is rubbed in until it evaporates and the hands are dry.

questions.text: The primary purpose of providing family support in palliative care is to:

options.B: Help them cope with grief and loss

questions.explanation: Help them cope with grief and loss (B) is correct because palliative care treats the patient and the family as a unit of care. The family faces anticipatory grief, fear, exhaustion and later bereavement, so support includes listening, explaining the illness in simple terms, involving them in care, spiritual and psychosocial support, and bereavement support after the death. Encouraging the family to leave quickly (A) is unkind and unethical, as families should be welcomed at the bedside. Giving medical instructions (C) is only a small part of support and is done by the nurse or clinician. Replacing professional care (D) is wrong because family members complement, but never replace, the professional care team.

questions.text: The role of an HCA in palliative care is:
questions.explanation: Providing emotional support (B) is correct because the HCA spends much time at the bedside, and in palliative care the role includes listening, showing empathy and respect, keeping the patient company, respecting culture and spiritual beliefs, helping with comfort needs (hygiene, mouth care, positioning, feeding), and reporting pain or distress to the nurse. Giving medications without supervision (A), administering chemotherapy (C) and performing diagnostic tests (D) are all outside the HCA's scope of practice and require a qualified nurse or clinician.

questions.text: A physical symptom commonly managed in palliative care is:
questions.explanation: Pain (C) is correct because pain is the most common and most feared physical symptom in patients with advanced illness such as cancer, and its relief is a central goal of palliative care, using the WHO analgesic ladder (non-opioids, weak opioids, strong opioids such as morphine) together with non-drug comfort measures. The HCA observes for signs of pain, including non-verbal signs in patients who cannot speak, and reports them promptly. Constipation (A) is also managed, mainly as a side effect of opioids, but pain is the leading symptom. Diarrhoea (B) is less common. Loneliness (D) is a psychosocial symptom, not a physical one.

questions.text: A normal change of aging in geriatric population is:
questions.explanation: Decrease in skin elasticity (B) is correct because with ageing the skin becomes thinner, drier and less elastic as collagen and elastin fibres decrease and subcutaneous fat is lost. This makes older people more prone to skin tears and pressure injuries, so the HCA handles them gently, keeps the skin clean and moisturised and repositions them regularly. Sudden loss of memory (A) is not normal and may indicate delirium, stroke or dementia. High fever (C) signals infection, and rapid weight gain (D) may indicate fluid retention from heart or kidney problems; none of these is a normal ageing change and they should be reported to the nurse.
